title: China proposes export controls on 23 AI technologies, open for public comment through November 15
subtitle: Announcement No. 48 from Beijing's commerce and science ministries would restrict transfers of large-model training methods, agent frameworks, and other AI know-how in the first mirror of US controls aimed at China's own stack.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology issued Announcement No. 48 on October 16, 2026, proposing to add 40 technologies to the national catalogue of items prohibited or restricted from export. Twenty-three of them are AI-related. The draft covers training methods and model weights for very large systems, agent frameworks, and related infrastructure. Public comments are open through November 15. Alongside the draft, an interim registration rule is already in force — any cross-border transfer of technology ownership, IP licensing, or change in control to overseas entities must be registered before it closes.

The mechanism matters. The thresholds reported in secondary coverage point to models at roughly two trillion parameters, training compute near 10^26 FLOPs, or a global top-ten rank — language that mirrors how the US has drawn its own lines. Carve-outs exist for technologies already in the public domain through open-source release or academic publication, and officials have said API access by overseas users is not covered. If the draft lands as written, Chinese labs would need government licenses to transfer frontier model know-how to foreign subsidiaries, partners, or customers.

For two years, the China-side AI export story was one of absorption: how fast could Chinese labs close the gap under US compute controls. Announcement 48 is the first time Beijing has publicly proposed to restrict its own frontier AI from leaving. It arrives weeks after the US trade truce began to fray, after a wave of open-weight releases from Chinese labs that reached Western developers, and after Zhipu's GLM-5.3 drew formal scrutiny from Apollo Research. Treat this as the Chinese counterpart to the US Entity List framework for AI, not as retaliation for any single action.

A note for learners: export controls are becoming a first-class constraint on the AI stack, next to compute and data. If you are building a product, read not just the US rules but also the Chinese ones — a model you license from a Chinese lab today may need an export license tomorrow, and your deployment plan has to account for that. The old assumption that frontier AI diffuses freely is ending.
